Executive Summary

This comprehensive report delivers an empirical and theoretical investigation into the systems challenges governing Large Language Model (LLM) serving. Using an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU on ASU's SOL supercomputer, we profile the asymmetric execution lifecycle of autoregressive transformers, quantify the exact performance and memory implications of Key-Value (KV) caching, explore batching scalability limits, and evaluate the head-of-line blocking phenomena induced by heterogeneous sequence lengths. We benchmark naive static batching against the modern high-throughput serving engine vLLM, demonstrate an 11.9× throughput acceleration (56.44 vs 4.74 req/s), design a production serving policy meeting rigorous Service Level Objectives (P95(TTFT) < 1.0 s, P95(TPOT) < 50 ms), and articulate why LLM serving is fundamentally an operating systems and scheduling discipline.

Part 0. Hardware / Software Environment & Timing Methodology

1. Experimental Environment and Controls

All benchmarks were performed on a dedicated compute node on the ASU SOL supercomputer running Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8.10. Software versions were strictly managed to ensure zero C++ ABI symbol mismatches across CUDA and PyTorch runtimes:

  • Host Hardware: AMD EPYC 7713 64-Core Processor, 512 GB Host DDR4 RAM.
  • GPU Accelerator: NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB (Compute Capability 8.0, 79.28 GiB VRAM, 1.935 TB/s memory bandwidth, 312 TFLOPS BF16 Tensor Core throughput).
  • Software Environment: Python 3.13.11 (Miniconda), CUDA 12.8, PyTorch 2.9.1, Transformers 5.12.1, vLLM 0.15.1, NumPy 2.2.6.
  • Model & Numerical Precision: Base architecture gpt2 (124M parameters, 12 layers, 12 heads, dmodel=768) strictly fixed to 16-bit half precision (torch.float16, b=2 bytes per element) across all PyTorch and vLLM benchmarks to satisfy the Part 0 requirement of fixed precision across comparisons.
  • Warm-Up & Repetition Policy: Every benchmark executed a minimum of 1 full forward-pass warm-up run prior to measurement to trigger kernel JIT compilation, CUDA context allocation, and page fault resolution. All reported metrics represent the arithmetic mean of 3 clean iterations.
  • Latency Isolation: Model weight loading, deserialization, and tokenizer initialization were strictly isolated and excluded from latency accounting.

2. Question 0.1: Analysis of Asynchronous CUDA Timing

Consider the following naive benchmarking snippet: 

start = time.perf_counter()
output = model(input_ids)
end = time.perf_counter()

Flaw in the Naive Implementation: In PyTorch, GPU kernel dispatches are inherently asynchronous with respect to the host CPU thread. Calling model(input_ids) simply constructs GPU command packets and pushes them onto the hardware CUDA stream queue. The host CPU thread immediately returns to Python without waiting for the streaming multiprocessors (SMs) to actually execute the matrix multiplications. As a result, time.perf_counter() measures only the CPU enqueue latency (often tens of microseconds), completely divorcing recorded timing from physical device computation. Furthermore, any previously queued background kernels will distort the measured window.

The Role of torch.cuda.synchronize(): torch.cuda.synchronize() serves as an explicit CPU-GPU barrier:

  • Calling it before start flushes all pending hardware queues, ensuring a clean measurement baseline.
  • Calling it before end halts CPU execution until the physical GPU has drained its work queue, processed all attention layers, and written valid results to memory.
A100 Empirical Verification: On our A100 GPU, naive asynchronous execution reported an elapsed time of 9.1998 ms (dominated by CPU driver dispatch overhead), whereas synchronized execution measured the true physical GPU execution of 7.1706 ms. Without proper synchronization, timing benchmarks are fundamentally invalid.

3. Starter Code Engineering Audit & Precision Control

A rigorous systems evaluation demands strict experimental controls. During our profiling, we identified and remediated critical architectural and environment edge cases in the starter code:

  1. Precision Drift Remediation (Part 0 Rule 5 & Common Pitfalls): Page 3 explicitly mandates: "Use the same model and numerical precision when comparing configurations," reinforced by Page 12: "Keep model and precision fixed across comparisons." In part4_static_batching.py, weights were loaded in torch.float16. However, the starter part4_vllm_offline.py invoked LLM(model=args.model) without passing a dtype argument, causing vLLM on our A100 GPU to default to dtype="auto" and automatically downcast FP32 weights to bfloat16. We resolved this precision drift by adding an explicit --dtype float16 CLI argument, guaranteeing that naive static batching and modern vLLM serve the exact same FP16 model weights and KV activations (b=2 bytes per element) for 100% fair experimental control.
  2. GPT-2 Absolute Context Window Boundary Guard: The GPT-2 architecture employs fixed absolute learned position embeddings (wpe of shape [1024, 768]). In the starter code, unbounded prompt and output length combinations (e.g., N + M > 1024) cause immediate CUDA index out-of-bounds assertions. We implemented dynamic position embedding guards (max_pos = getattr(model.config, 'max_position_embeddings', 1024)) across Parts 1 and 4, enabling stress-testing up to 100% context capacity (N=768, M=256 ⇒ 1024) without runtime failure.
  3. C++ ABI Symbol Resolution & Runtime Isolation: On the SOL supercomputer, automatic dependency resolution linked PyTorch against unused multimodal packages (torchvision, torchaudio), triggering undefined C++ ABI operator symbol conflicts (_ZN3c104cuda29c10_cuda_check_implementation...). We pinned PyTorch to torch==2.9.1+cu128 and masked multimodal dependencies in part4_vllm_offline.py, ensuring clean text LLM execution.

3. Detailed Task 1.3 Analysis

  1. Why Prompt Length Affects Prefill: Prefill processes all N input tokens simultaneously in a single forward pass. Computing multi-head attention requires evaluating pairwise token affinities: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q KT / √d) V. The matrix multiplication Q KT between [N, d_k] and [d_k, N] scales quadratically as O(N2) in FLOPs and attention matrix size, while linear feed-forward projections scale as O(N · dmodel2). Consequently, prefill latency and intermediate activation memory grow directly with prompt length.
  2. Why Output Length Affects Decode: Autoregressive generation is strictly sequential: token yi cannot be predicted until token yi-1 has been sampled and projected into embedding space. Generating M tokens mandates M distinct forward passes through all 12 transformer layers. Total decode latency scales linearly with output length: Decode Latency ≈ M × TPOT (e.g., 199.4 ms for M=32, 805.3 ms for M=128, and 1617.5 ms for M=256).
  3. Why Prefill Exposes Far More Parallelism Than Decode: In prefill, all N tokens are available upfront. Matrix multiplications are batched General Matrix Multiplies (GEMMs) of dimensions [N, dmodel] × [dmodel, 4dmodel], saturating the 432 Tensor Cores of the A100. In decode, generating one token at a time reduces tensor operations to Matrix-Vector multiplies (GEMVs) of shape [1, dmodel], leaving the vast majority of GPU execution units idle while waiting on memory fetches.
  4. Compute vs. Memory Bandwidth Sensitivity:
    • Prefill is Compute-Bound: Each parameter loaded from High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is reused across all N tokens in parallel, giving prefill high arithmetic intensity (FLOPs/byte) that places it on the flat roofline ceiling of the A100.
    • Decode is Memory-Bandwidth Bound: In single-token decode, the entire 124M parameter tensor (~250 MB in FP16) must be transferred from HBM to SM registers to generate a single token. Decoding 1 token requires ≈ 2 × 124M FLOPs, resulting in an arithmetic intensity of ≈ 1 FLOP/byte, severely bounded by memory bus bandwidth.
  5. Does TPOT Remain Constant as Context Grows? On our A100, GPT-2 TPOT remains exceptionally stable across context lengths (~6.28–6.35 ms/token) because streaming 124M weights (~250 MB) dominates over the tiny GPT-2 KV cache (~36 MB at 1024 tokens). However, as context lengths reach 8K–32K tokens in larger models, the KV cache footprint exceeds model weights, causing memory bus saturation and driving TPOT upward.

3. Task 2.3: KV-Cache Memory Formula Derivation

Let the transformer serving parameters be defined as:

  • B: Number of concurrent sequences (batch size).
  • L: Number of transformer layers in the model architecture.
  • S: Total sequence context length (prompt tokens N + generated tokens M).
  • HKV: Number of key-value attention heads (equal to total attention heads H in Multi-Head Attention, or a fraction in Grouped-Query Attention).
  • D: Head projection dimension (dhead = dmodel / H).
  • b: Precision storage size in bytes per numerical element (b = 2 for FP16 and BF16; b = 1 for FP8).
Closed-Form Formula:
MKV = 2 × B × L × S × HKV × D × b   [Bytes]

Step-by-Step Derivation:

  1. At each token position s ∈ [1, S], the self-attention mechanism projects hidden states into Key and Value vectors: K = X WK and V = X WV.
  2. Per token per layer, the Key representation contains HKV × D floating-point scalars, and the Value representation contains HKV × D floating-point scalars, totaling 2 × HKV × D elements.
  3. For a sequence of length S, the cumulative elements stored across all L layers equals 2 × L × S × HKV × D.
  4. Serving B concurrent sequences requires scaling by B, yielding total elements 2 × B × L × S × HKV × D.
  5. Multiplying total elements by the data type precision b (2 bytes for FP16/BF16) produces the exact byte footprint MKV.

Explanation of the Factor of 2: In the scaled dot-product attention equation: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax((Q KT) / √D) V, the model computes query-key affinities to determine attention weights, and then takes the weighted sum over value vectors. To compute attention for new token yt without re-evaluating past tokens, the system must retain both Keys (to compute affinity scores) and Values (to compute output representations) independently. Storing two distinct tensors (K and V) for every token introduces the fundamental factor of 2.

4. Sizing Calculations & Verification via part2_kv_size.py

  • LLaMA-Style 7B Model (B=1, L=32, S=4096, HKV=8, D=128, b=2): MKV = 2 × 1 × 32 × 4096 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 536,870,912 Bytes = 0.5000 GiB per request. At high concurrency (B=64), the KV cache requires 32.00 GiB, exceeding the entire model weight footprint (14 GB)!
  • GPT-2 Base Model (B=1, L=12, S=1024, HKV=12, D=64, b=2): MKV = 2 × 1 × 12 × 1024 × 12 × 64 × 2 = 37,748,736 Bytes = 36.00 MiB.

5. Task 2.4 Analysis

  • Why Caching Reduces Redundant Computation: Without caching, step t must recompute query, key, value projections and attention across all t-1 prior tokens across all layers, incurring O(M · N2 + M3) FLOPs. With caching, preceding keys and values are retained in memory, reducing per-token decoding to O(1) projections and O(S) attention reads.
  • Why Memory Footprint Grows Linearly with Sequence Length: Because self-attention requires every token to attend to the entire historical sequence, each newly generated token appends new K and V vectors. The cache footprint cannot be compressed or discarded without sacrificing exact model outputs.
  • Why Long Context Limits Serving Concurrency: Fixed GPU memory (80 GB on our A100) must hold weights, runtime activations, and KV caches. Because KV cache memory scales as O(B · S), increasing context length S forces concurrency Bmax ∝ 1/S to drop precipitously.
  • Why Systems Hit Memory Limits Before Compute Limits: Under long-context workloads, the dynamic KV cache consumes 80–90% of available VRAM, causing out-of-memory (OOM) allocation failures even when GPU Tensor Core utilization is under 20%.

3. Task 3.3 Analysis & Metric Verification (TODO 2)

  1. Verification of Metric Formulas (TODO 2):
    • requests_per_sec = batch_size / total_sec: Accurately reflects the rate of completed requests returned to users over the benchmark interval.
    • tokens_per_sec = (batch_size * output_length) / total_sec: Captures the aggregate generative output bandwidth across all concurrent streams.
    • tpot_ms = decode_sec * 1000 / output_length: Accurately measures the mean duration required to generate each successive output token across the batch.
  2. Why Larger Batches Improve GPU Utilization: At batch size 1, decoding streams 124M weights to process a single token, operating far below GPU compute capacity. Increasing batch size from 1 to 16 batches 16 tokens together, amortizing the cost of reading weights across 16 parallel vectors. This shifts decoding from memory-bound GEMVs to compute-dense GEMMs, boosting token throughput by 16.6× (from 158.98 to 2641.17 tokens/s) while latency remains completely flat (~0.77–0.80 s).
  3. Why Throughput Cannot Grow Indefinitely: As batch size increases further, two physical bottlenecks emerge: (1) Compute Saturation: Tensor Cores reach peak FLOP capacity, causing per-iteration compute time to scale linearly with B; (2) KV Cache Bandwidth: Loading B distinct KV cache tensors saturates HBM bus bandwidth.
  4. The Latency-Throughput Tradeoff: Throughput measures global system output, whereas latency measures single-request response time. Under compute-saturated models, batching increases per-step iteration duration, degrading individual user latency to achieve higher collective throughput.
  5. Chatbot Serving Configuration: An interactive chatbot service would not select the maximum throughput batch size. Chatbots require strict SLAs (P95(TPOT) < 50 ms, TTFT < 1.0 s) for natural conversational reading speed. High-throughput static batching induces severe queue wait times that violate interactive user experience.

2. Tasks 4.1 & 4.2 Analysis: Structural Flaws of Static Batching

  • Prompt Padding Waste (Task 4.1): Consider a batch with prompt lengths 128, 150, 180, and 1024 tokens. Static batching pads all sequences to max_len = 1024:
    Useful Tokens = 128 + 150 + 180 + 1024 = 1482 tokens.
    Padded Tokens = 4 × 1024 = 4096 tokens.
    Padding Efficiency = 1482 / 4096 = 36.18%. Over 63.8% of memory and compute is wasted on dummy pad tokens.
  • Output-Length Heterogeneity (Task 4.2): Consider output lengths of 20, 25, 200, and 30 tokens. Requests 1, 2, and 4 terminate generation at steps 20, 25, and 30 upon emitting <EOS>. However, static batching traps all four requests in the execution batch until request 3 finishes step 200. For 170 steps (85% of total run time), 75% of batch capacity computes useless dummy tokens while locking up GPU VRAM.
  • Dynamic Early Exit (TODO 3): Iteration-level scheduling allows completed sequences to exit immediately upon emitting <EOS>, reclaiming their memory and slotting waiting requests into the active batch dynamically.
  • Pitfalls of Uniform max_tokens (TODO 4): Setting a uniform max_tokens masks output heterogeneity in artificial benchmarks, failing to expose the severe head-of-line blocking observed in real conversational traffic.

3. Modern Systems Mechanisms (Task 4.4)

  • Continuous Batching (Orca): Iteration-level scheduling eliminates the boundary of static request batches. Completed requests are evicted immediately, and new requests enter the decode pool at every single forward pass, maintaining near-100% GPU saturation.
  • Paged KV-Cache Management (PagedAttention / vLLM): Inspired by virtual memory paging in operating systems, PagedAttention divides the KV cache into fixed-size physical memory blocks (16 tokens). Blocks are allocated dynamically on-demand, completely eliminating external fragmentation and reducing internal memory waste to below 4%. This enables 2× to 4× higher concurrency in the exact same physical VRAM.
